abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Sustainable agricultural production requires approaches that improve resource-use efficiency while limiting environmental burdens. This critical review examines green-synthesized Nanoparticles (NPs) in precision agriculture, covering sustainable synthesis, smart crop management, nano-enabled delivery systems, nano-biosensors, plant-nanoparticle interactions, environmental risks, circular agriculture, and digital technologies. The NPs derived from Plant, microbial, biomolecule, and waste shows potential for targeted nutrient delivery, crop protection, stress management, and improved monitoring. However, reported performance varies with NP size, surface properties, concentration, formulation, crop type, soil, and environmental conditions. The review therefore critically considers both benefits and risks, including phytotoxicity, effects on beneficial microorganisms, persistence, bioaccumulation, and long-term ecosystem impacts. Waste-derived NPs and circular nanomanufacturing offer opportunities for resource recovery and agricultural waste valorization, but their scalability and economic feasibility remain uncertain. The integration with Artificial Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoTs), Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), remote sensing, and smart decision-support systems may improve site-specific management. The review also examines technology readiness, commercialization pathways, manufacturing consistency, cost, and regulatory requirements. The green NPs shows promise for sustainable precision agriculture, but wider adoption requires stronger field validation, standardized characterization, environmental risk assessment, reproducible manufacturing, economic evaluation, and responsible regulatory development.

list-item.p: This review examines how green NPs can support precision agriculture through improved nutrient delivery, crop protection, stress management, and more efficient resource use.
The reviewed studies show that nano-based delivery systems, sensors, and digital technologies can improve targeted input application, crop monitoring, and data-based crop management.
The review shows that plant-nanoparticle interactions and possible effects on soil, water, beneficial organisms, and the wider environment must be considered alongside agricultural benefits.
Waste-derived NPs and circular farming approaches can support waste recovery and resource reuse, but their effectiveness and environmental safety need careful evaluation before wider application.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Modern agriculture must increase food production to meet the growing demand for food while reducing environmental impacts and using limited land and water resources efficiently.1 Climate variability, soil degradation, and growing pressure on natural resources make this increasingly difficult.2 In many conventional farming systems, fertilisers, water, and pesticides are applied evenly across whole fields even though soil and crop conditions are not the same everywhere. This can lead to nutrient loss through leaching and runoff, unnecessary use of agrochemicals, higher greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, and poor use of resources.3,4 Future farming therefore needs better ways to use water, nutrients, and crop-protection products while maintaining crop production.5

Precision agriculture (PA) has developed to address these problems and it uses technologies such as remote sensing, Global Positioning System (GPS), Variable Rate Technology (VRT), and Internet of Things (IoT) systems to apply farm inputs according to actual field conditions.4 Satellites and Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) provide information on crop health, soil moisture, nutrient status, and pest occurrence. GIS can then be used to map this information and guide field operations.3,6 GPS-guided equipment improves the accuracy of sowing, fertiliser application, and harvesting, while VRT allows water, nutrients, and pesticides to be applied at different rates within the same field.4 Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and big-data analysis are now also being used to support decisions on irrigation, fertilisation, pest control, and harvesting.3,7 Reported studies indicate water savings of 20–50% and fertiliser reductions of 15–30% while maintaining or increasing yields.8 However, high costs, technical difficulties, and limited digital infrastructure still restrict wider use of these technologies.3,7 More importantly, PA can show where a problem exists, but the required input must still be delivered accurately and at the right time.

Green-synthesised nanoparticles (NPs) may help to address the above stated problem. Nanoparticles are generally smaller than 100 nm and have properties that differ from larger particles because of their small size and large surface area.9 Conventional methods for producing NPs include chemical precipitation, sol-gel, solvothermal, and hydrothermal processes. These methods may require high energy input and hazardous chemicals.9,10 Green synthesis uses plant extracts, microorganisms, or biomolecules to form and stabilise NPs.9,11 Plant materials contain compounds such as flavonoids, proteins, polysaccharides, and alkaloids that can help in NP formation. Alternatively, bacteria, fungi, algae, and other biological materials can also be used.11,12 Agricultural wastes, such as fallen leaves, can also serve as raw materials, linking NP production with waste use and circular agriculture.10 These methods can reduce the need for hazardous chemicals, but the final properties and performance of the NPs still depend on the source material and the conditions used during synthesis.5,13

Green NPs are being studied for several agricultural uses. In nutrient management, nano-fertilisers and nano-carriers can provide nutrients slowly and in a more controlled manner, which may improve nutrient-use efficiency.12,13 Green-synthesised silver (Ag), Copper Oxide (CuO), Titanium dioxide (TiO2), and Zinc Oxide (ZnO) NPs have shown antifungal, antibacterial, and nematicidal effects.12,14 Silica nanoparticle-coated biochar has also been reported to reduce Fusarium oxysporum infection in crops and to activate plant defence responses.15 Nano-enabled delivery systems can release active substances in a controlled and targeted way. Nanoparticles have also been studied for improving plant responses to drought, salinity, metal stress, and other environmental stresses.15,16 At the same time, nano-biosensors are being developed to detect plant stress, pathogens, pesticide residues, and nutrient status at an early stage. Some of these sensors are being combined with portable devices and AI-based systems for field use.17–19

The reported benefits of green NPs are not the same in every situation. Their effects depend on particle size, surface properties, charge, concentration, formulation, crop species, soil type, and environmental conditions.15,16,20 The dose is also important, for example, nano-Fe-modified biochar reduced cadmium toxicity at 0.2–0.4% application rates but increased cadmium toxicity in leaves at 0.8–1.6%.21 This shows that a higher dose does not always give a better result. There are also concerns about environmental safety, the Ag NPs may affect useful soil microorganisms such as Rhizobium and Glomus species. Nanoparticle accumulation in plants has also been linked with oxidative stress, reduced photosynthesis, poor root and shoot growth, delayed germination, and genetic damage.22,23 Their movement and persistence in soil can also change with particle size, surface coating, and environmental ageing and the long-term field information is still limited.20 In addition, problems related to scale-up, batch consistency, production cost, characterisation cost, and regulation continue to limit wider use.16,24–26

The main problem is that the available evidence is scattered across different topics. Some studies focus on NP synthesis, others on nutrient delivery, disease control, stress management, or sensing. Many are carried out in laboratories or greenhouses and under a limited range of crop and soil conditions. There is still limited field-scale evidence, limited information on nanoparticle interactions with soil, microbes, and plants under real farming conditions, and limited agreement on methods for nanoparticle characterisation and testing. Information on life-cycle impacts and what happens to nano-enabled inputs after use is also limited.16,20,27

This review examines how green-synthesised NPs can be used in PA and what is needed for their safe and practical use. It covers green synthesis using plants, microorganisms, biomolecules, and agricultural wastes; nutrient management; crop protection; stress management; nano-enabled delivery systems; nano-biosensors; plant–nanoparticle interactions; environmental effects; circular agriculture; AI and digital farming; technology readiness; manufacturing; cost; commercialisation; and regulation.

The review addresses five main questions: (1) How do green synthesis methods and nanoparticle properties influence agricultural performance? (2) What benefits, limitations, and mechanisms have been reported for the major agricultural applications of green nanoparticles? (3) What are the main environmental and biological concerns related to nanoparticle toxicity, environmental fate, accumulation, and effects on plants and ecosystems? (4) How can green nanoparticles be integrated with precision agriculture, digital technologies, and circular agriculture? (5) What scientific, technical, economic, regulatory, field-validation, and scale-up challenges must be addressed for the practical and responsible use of green nanoparticles in agriculture?

The main contribution of this review is its focus on green-synthesised NPs within the broader precision-agriculture framework, linking their synthesis and agricultural functions with smart crop management, nano-enabled delivery, nano-biosensors, plant–nanoparticle interactions, environmental safety, digital agriculture, and circular resource use. The review further examines the evidence needed to move these technologies from laboratory and controlled studies towards field application by considering technology readiness, scale-up, economic feasibility, manufacturing consistency, commercialisation, and regulatory requirements. Rather than presenting these areas separately, the review examines their connections and identifies the key scientific, technical, environmental, and practical gaps that must be addressed for responsible agricultural application.

sec.p: A Population-Intervention-Comparison-Outcome (PICO) framework was used to define the review scope and guide the identification, selection, and synthesis of relevant literature. The framework was adapted to examine green-synthesised NPs in PA, covering sustainable synthesis, smart crop management, nano-enabled delivery, precision sensing, plant-nanoparticle interactions, environmental sustainability, and circular agriculture. sec.title: Inclusion, Exclusion Criteria and Study Selection
sec.p: The literature was selected based on its relevance to green-synthesised NPs and their agricultural applications. Eligible studies included peer-reviewed articles, reviews, book chapters, and conference proceedings addressing nanoparticle synthesis, characterisation, agricultural applications, environmental effects, or sustainability. Studies unrelated to agriculture, focused solely on industrial applications, non-English publications, duplicates, and records with insufficient technical information were excluded. Retrieved records were managed in Zotero reference manager, where duplicates were removed before title, abstract, and full-text screening. Studies were retained when they addressed green-synthesised NPs and at least one defined agricultural outcome within the review scope. Additional studies were identified through backward and forward reference tracking, and the selected literature was grouped according to the major review themes. As this is a narrative critical review rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis, the findings were critically synthesised rather than statistically pooled. The main limitations include differences in nanoparticle properties, experimental conditions, crop and soil systems, and the limited field evidence available for some applications.

sec.title: Evidence Synthesis and Critical Appraisal
sec.p: The selected literature was critically synthesized according to the major themes of the review, including green synthesis, nutrient management, crop protection, stress management, nano-enabled delivery systems, nano-biosensors, plant-nanoparticle interactions, environmental impacts, circular agriculture, and technology readiness. For each theme, findings were compared according to nanoparticle type, synthesis route, particle characteristics, concentration, application method, crop or biological system, experimental conditions, and reported outcomes. Greater emphasis was given to studies providing clear experimental methods, nanoparticle characterization, appropriate controls, quantitative results, and evidence from field or semi-field conditions. Findings were interpreted by identifying consistent results, contrasting observations, and important limitations across studies. Conclusions were then developed from the overall pattern of evidence rather than from individual studies, with particular attention to the strength of evidence, uncertainties, and the extent to which laboratory findings had been validated under realistic agricultural conditions.

sec.title: Green Synthesis of Nanoparticles for Agricultural Applications
Plant-Mediated Synthesis
sec.p: Plant-mediated synthesis of NPs using phytochemicals and agricultural biomass offers a sustainable and reduced chemical use alternative to conventional chemical and physical methods, which often involve harsh conditions and toxic chemicals. This green synthesis approach leverages the natural reducing and stabilizing properties of plant extracts, which contain phytochemicals such as phenolic compounds, terpenoids, and proteins, to produce NPs with enhanced stability and uniformity.28,29 The use of agricultural biomass and plant extracts not only reduces the environmental burden but also utilizes renewable resources, making the process cost-effective and sustainable.30 This method has been successfully applied to synthesize various NPs, including Copper (Cu), Silver (Ag), and Zinc (Zn), which have significant applications in agriculture, such as enhancing plant growth, improving disease resistance, and acting as nano-fertilizers.28,31,32 For example, Cu NPs have been shown to increase root and shoot growth in mung beans and enhance grain yield and stress tolerance in wheat.28 Similarly, Ag NPs synthesized using plant extracts have demonstrated antimicrobial properties against phytopathogens, offering a green solution for managing agricultural diseases.33 The integration of these NPs into precision farming systems can optimize nutrient delivery and pest control, thereby improving crop yield and quality while minimizing environmental impact.34,35 Moreover, the use of endophytic microbiomes and other biological synthesis pathways enhances the sustainability of nanoparticle production, contributing to more resilient agricultural systems.36 The plant-mediated synthesis of NPs aligns with the principles of PA by providing site-specific, need-based solutions that enhance agricultural productivity and sustainability.32

sec.title: Microbial and Biomolecule-Assisted Synthesis
sec.p: Microbial and biomolecule-assisted nanoparticle synthesis approaches are increasingly recognized for their eco-friendly characteristics, controlled synthesis capabilities, and relevance to sustainable agricultural applications. These methods leverage the natural metabolic processes of microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, algae, and even plant-derived biomolecules to produce NPs in a manner that is both environmentally benign and cost-effective. Unlike traditional chemical and physical synthesis methods, which often involve toxic reagents and high energy consumption, biological synthesis routes are sustainable and reduce environmental toxicity.37–39 Microbial synthesis, in particular, offers advantages such as scalability and the ability to produce NPs with tunable size, shape, and surface properties through enzymatic and metabolic processes.40 This approach is not only eco-friendly but also allows for precise control over NP characteristics, which is crucial for their application in agriculture.41,42 In sustainable agriculture, these biologically synthesized NPs can be used as nano-fertilizers, nano-pesticides, and plant growth stimulators, enhancing plant growth and resistance to diseases while minimizing the use of harmful agrochemicals.36,43 For example, Trichoderma-mediated NPs have been applied as nano-fungicides and plant growth stimulators, demonstrating their potential in agri-food applications.37 Moreover, the integration of nanotechnology in agriculture through these green synthesis methods can lead to the development of smart delivery systems for nutrients and pesticides, thereby improving crop productivity and sustainability.44 The use of endophytic microbiomes for NP synthesis is another promising approach, offering reduced chemical use alternatives that enhance plant growth and disease resistance.36 The microbial and biomolecule-assisted NP synthesis not only aligns with the principles of green chemistry but also holds significant promise for advancing sustainable agricultural practices by improving crop yields and reducing environmental impact.45

sec.title: Sustainability-Relevant Characteristics of Green Nanoparticles
sec.p: Green NPs, synthesized through eco-friendly methods, exhibit several sustainability-related properties that make them highly suitable for precision agricultural applications. These NPs are characterized by their biodegradability and biocompatibility, which are crucial for minimizing environmental impact and ensuring safety for both plants and soil ecosystems. The use of natural polymers and biological resources in their synthesis, such as polysaccharides and plant extracts, enhances their biodegradability and reduces toxicity, making them a safer alternative to conventional agrochemicals.46,47 Green NPs also demonstrate reduced toxicity due to the absence of harmful chemicals in their synthesis process, which aligns with the principles of green chemistry and minimizes the risk of environmental contamination.47,48 Their environmental compatibility is further underscored by their ability to degrade into non-toxic by-products, such as bioavailable monosilicic acid in the case of Silica (Si) NPs, which enriches soil health and supports beneficial microbial communities.49 In PA, these NPs offer significant advantages, including enhanced nutrient delivery systems, improved stress tolerance, and reduced dependency on synthetic inputs. For example, ZnO NPs and Si NPs have been shown to improve nutrient use efficiency and bolster plant resilience against abiotic and biotic stresses, thereby supporting sustainable agricultural practices.32,49 Additionally, the encapsulation of natural compounds within polysaccharide-based NPs allows for controlled release and precise dosage, reducing the risk of treatment resistance and minimizing the negative effects of chemical fertilizers and pesticides.46 The integration of green NPs in agriculture not only promotes environmental sustainability but also enhances crop productivity and resilience, aligning with global sustainability goals.48,49

Although green synthesis can reduce the use of hazardous reagents and make use of renewable biological resources, these advantages do not automatically establish lower environmental impact or better agricultural performance. The properties of the resulting NPs depend strongly on the biological source, synthesis conditions, particle size, surface chemistry, and post-synthesis processing. Consequently, NPs produced through the same general green route may show different stability, biological activity, and toxicity. The literature therefore supports viewing green synthesis as a potentially lower-impact production approach rather than as evidence of inherent environmental safety or sustainability. Table 3 summarizes the major green synthesis routes employed for the production of agricultural NPs and highlights their associated sustainability characteristics, advantages, and agricultural relevance. The table demonstrates that plant-mediated, agro-waste-mediated, microbial, and biomolecule-assisted synthesis methods provide environmentally responsible alternatives to conventional nanoparticle production by utilizing renewable biological resources, reducing chemical consumption, and operating under mild reaction conditions. Plant-derived and agro-waste-based approaches contribute directly to circular agriculture through biomass valorization and resource recovery, while microbial and algal synthesis offer low-toxicity and energy-efficient pathways for nanoparticle production. Biomolecule-assisted routes, including protein-, polysaccharide-, and enzyme-mediated synthesis, further enhance nanoparticle biocompatibility, biodegradability, stability, and controlled-release functionality, making them particularly suitable for nano-enabled agricultural delivery systems. The resulting NPs, including Ag, ZnO, Cu, iron oxide, Si, and polymeric nanomaterials, support diverse agricultural applications such as nano-fertilization, crop protection, stress management, smart delivery systems, and precision farming technologies. Collectively, the synthesis routes presented illustrates how green nanotechnology integrates sustainable production, circular resource utilization, and agricultural functionality, providing a foundation for the development of environmentally compatible nanoparticle systems that enhance crop productivity while minimizing ecological impacts.

sec.p: Figure 2 illustrates the major green synthesis pathways used for the production of agricultural NPs, highlighting the progression from biological resources to sustainable agricultural applications. The framework shows that plant materials, microorganisms, and naturally occurring biomolecules serve as the primary sources of reducing and stabilizing agents required for nanoparticle synthesis. Bioactive compounds derived from these sources facilitate the reduction of metal ions, followed by nucleation, growth, capping, and stabilization processes that govern nanoparticle formation, size, morphology, and stability. Through these mechanisms, a variety of NPs, including Ag, ZnO, Cu, iron oxide, and Si NPs, can be synthesized without the extensive use of hazardous chemicals. The illustration further emphasizes that green-synthesized NPs possess sustainability-relevant characteristics such as biocompatibility, biodegradability, low toxicity, renewable feedstock utilization, and reduced chemical consumption, making them more environmentally compatible than conventional nanomaterials. These attributes support their application in PA through nano-fertilizers, nano-pesticides, precision nutrient delivery, plant growth promotion, disease management, and stress tolerance enhancement. The framework demonstrates how green synthesis integrates biological resources, environmentally benign production processes, and sustainable agricultural functions, thereby supporting the development of resource-efficient and environmentally responsible nano-enabled farming systems.

sec.title: Green Nanoparticles in Smart Crop Management
Precision Nutrient Delivery Systems
sec.p: Green NPs have emerged as a promising approach in precision nutrient delivery systems, offering controlled nutrient release, enhanced nutrient-use efficiency, reduced fertilizer loss, and sustainable crop productivity. The application of nano-fertilizers, such as nano-DAP, has demonstrated significant improvements in nutrient use efficiency and crop yield. For example, a study on rainfed maize showed that using nano-DAP alongside conventional fertilizers could reduce nitrogen and phosphorus inputs by 25% without compromising yield or profitability, while also reducing greenhouse gas emissions and energy consumption.55 Si NPs further enhance nutrient delivery by providing controlled and sustained release mechanisms, which minimize nutrient losses and ensure consistent crop uptake. SiNPs also improve plant resilience against abiotic stresses and reduce dependency on conventional agrochemicals, aligning with sustainability goals.49 The development of Nano-Biochar-Coated Slow-Release Fertilizers (NBC-SRF) exemplifies the potential of NPs in extending nutrient availability and improving water retention, thereby enhancing nutrient use efficiency and environmental sustainability.56 Similarly, chitosan xerogels embedded with cerium oxide NPs offer controlled release of nutrients, improving plant growth and reducing environmental impact.57 Nanophotonic fertilizers, which integrate light conversion and nutrient delivery, have shown to significantly enhance photosynthetic performance and biomass, demonstrating the multifunctional capabilities of NPs in agriculture.58 Nanohybrid fertilizers, which incorporate nanotechnology into traditional fertilizer matrices, enable precise control over nutrient release, reducing nutrient runoff and environmental pollution while improving crop yields.59 Bio-nano-fertilizers, combining nanoscale materials with beneficial microorganisms, further enhance nutrient uptake and soil health, offering a sustainable alternative to chemical fertilizers.60 Collectively, these advancements in green nanoparticle applications underscore their important role in advancing PA, promoting sustainable crop productivity, and mitigating the environmental impacts of traditional fertilization practices.

sec.title: Smart Pest and Disease Management
sec.p: Nano-enabled pesticide and antimicrobial delivery systems utilizing green NPs present a promising approach for targeted pest and disease control, significantly reducing the need for excessive agrochemical application and minimizing environmental contamination. These systems leverage the unique properties of NPs, such as increased surface area and enhanced chemical effectiveness, to improve the delivery and efficacy of active ingredients in pesticides and antimicrobials.61 The development of multifunctional NPs and nano-pesticides has shown to enhance absorption and conduction by plants, improve efficacy, reduce dosage, and delay resistance, while also protecting beneficial insects and reducing residues.62 These advancements are crucial in addressing the adverse effects of conventional pesticides, which include environmental pollution, health risks, and soil microbiota disruption.63 Green synthesis of nano-agrochemicals, which emphasizes eco-friendly and sustainable practices, further enhances the potential of these systems to transform agriculture by increasing crop yields and reducing environmental contamination.64 Controlled Release Systems (CRSs) based on nanocarriers offer an eco-efficient strategy for the precise delivery of agrochemicals, responding to specific environmental stimuli and reducing premature loss of active ingredients.65 Moreover, the integration of nanotechnology in agriculture facilitates the development of smart delivery systems that can target specific pathogens and pests, thereby improving biosafety and reducing collateral damage to non-target organisms.66,67 Despite these promising developments, the commercial application of nano-enabled systems in agriculture remains limited, necessitating further research to assess ecological impacts and optimize delivery strategies.61 The strategic use of green NPs in pesticide and antimicrobial delivery systems holds significant potential for sustainable agriculture, enhancing food security while safeguarding environmental and human health.68,69

sec.title: Stress Management and Climate-Resilient Agriculture
sec.p: Green NPs play a pivotal role in enhancing plant tolerance to various environmental stresses, such as drought, salinity, and oxidative stress, which are critical for developing climate-resilient agricultural systems. These NPs, synthesized through reduced chemical use methods, possess unique physicochemical properties that enable them to penetrate plant tissues, thereby enhancing nutrient uptake and stress resistance.70,71 They mitigate the adverse effects of abiotic stressors by optimizing physiological and biochemical processes, such as photosynthesis, nutrient uptake, and water absorption, which are often disrupted under stress conditions.72 Specifically, NPs enhance the antioxidant defense systems in plants, thereby reducing oxidative stress caused by Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) and maintaining redox homeostasis.71,73 This is crucial as oxidative stress can impair plant growth and development. Moreover, NPs improve photosynthetic efficiency and protect cellular membranes, which are vital for maintaining plant health under drought and salinity stress.74,75 They also regulate gene expression and boost the accumulation of osmolytes, hormones, and phenolics, contributing to enhanced stress tolerance.74 The application of NPs in agriculture not only improves plant resilience but also promotes sustainable farming practices by reducing the need for conventional agrochemicals, thus minimizing environmental pollution.76,77 However, while the benefits of NPs are significant, there are concerns regarding their environmental and health impacts, necessitating further research to develop standardized application protocols and assess long-term effects.22,70 The integration of green NPs into agricultural systems offers a promising approach to enhance crop resilience and ensure food security in the face of climate change.72,78

sec.title: Crop Growth Enhancement and Yield Improvement
sec.p: Green NPs have emerged as a promising approach in precision farming systems, significantly influencing seed germination, nutrient uptake, photosynthesis, metabolic activity, and overall crop growth and productivity. Nanopriming, a technique involving the use of NPs, enhances seed germination by stimulating aquaporin expression and increasing amylase production, which facilitates starch degradation and water uptake, thereby improving seed vigor and stress tolerance throughout the plant’s lifecycle.79,80 The unique physicochemical properties of NPs, such as high surface-area-to-volume ratios, enable them to penetrate biological membranes effectively, allowing for targeted nutrient delivery and enhanced stress tolerance. This capability is crucial in mitigating abiotic stresses like drought, salinity, and heavy metal toxicity, which are major contributors to global yield losses.22,72 Nanoparticles also enhance photosynthetic efficiency and enzymatic activity, which are vital for plant growth and resilience under stress conditions.72,81 The application of nano-fertilizers, such as silica-based and carbon-based variants, improves nutrient retention, reduces runoff, and enhances nitrogen use efficiency, contributing to sustainable crop production.72,82 Moreover, NPs can modulate biochemical pathways and signalling mechanisms, promoting stress resistance and reducing the need for conventional pesticides and fertilizers.83 Despite these benefits, the long-term environmental impact and potential toxicity of NPs remain areas of concern, necessitating further research to develop standardized application protocols and ensure their safe integration into agricultural practices.22,81 The strategic use of green NPs in precision farming holds immense promise for enhancing crop productivity and sustainability, addressing the challenges posed by climate change and resource depletion.84,85

The reported agronomic benefits should, however, be interpreted with caution because nanoparticle responses are not uniform across crops, materials, concentrations, and growing conditions. Some studies report improvements in nutrient uptake, photosynthesis, stress tolerance, and yield, whereas excessive nanoparticle concentrations can produce phytotoxic effects and impair plant physiological processes. The evidence therefore suggests a concentration and context-dependent response rather than a universally positive effect. Differences in crop species, nanoparticle properties, application method, exposure duration, and environmental conditions also make direct comparison between studies difficult. These variations indicate that promising results obtained under controlled conditions cannot automatically be considered representative of field performance.

Figure 3 illustrates the role of green NPs in smart crop management by linking sustainable nanoparticle synthesis with key agricultural functions, plant responses, and farming outcomes. NPs produced through plant-mediated, microbial, and biomolecule-assisted synthesis routes are utilized in precision nutrient delivery, pest and disease management, stress mitigation, and crop growth enhancement. Their application improves nutrient-use efficiency through controlled nutrient release, supports targeted pest control with reduced agrochemical inputs, and enhances plant tolerance to drought, salinity, and oxidative stress through the activation of stress-responsive defense mechanisms. These functions collectively influence plant physiological and biochemical processes, including nutrient uptake, photosynthetic regulation, enzyme activation, water-use efficiency, and stress tolerance. The resulting improvements contribute to higher crop productivity, enhanced yield and crop quality, and increased resilience under variable environmental conditions. At the farming-system level, these benefits translate into greater resource-use efficiency through reduced fertilizer and pesticide losses, optimized input utilization, and lower environmental burdens. The framework demonstrates how green NPs can support sustainable crop production by integrating precision management strategies with improved plant performance and environmental sustainability objectives.

sec.title: Nano-Enabled Delivery Systems in Precision Agriculture
Controlled and Targeted Agrochemical Delivery
sec.p: The development of nano-enabled delivery systems for fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides represents a promising development in agricultural technology, focusing on controlled release, target specificity, reduced chemical losses, and improved agricultural efficiency. These systems utilize nanocarriers such as synthetic and natural polymers, nano-emulsions, lipid NPs, and nanofibers to create Controlled Release Systems (CRSs) that are eco-friendly and reduce environmental pollution and health risks associated with conventional agrochemicals.65 Nano-fertilizers, for example, are engineered to enhance nutrient uptake efficiency by delivering macro- and micronutrients directly to the plant rhizosphere in a regulated manner, thus improving nutrient management and reducing environmental impact.82,92 Similarly, nano-pesticides and nano-herbicides are designed to provide targeted delivery and controlled release, which significantly enhances their efficacy while minimizing non-target effects and environmental contamination.68,93 The integration of smart, stimuli-responsive release mechanisms allows these nano-based pesticides to respond to specific environmental triggers, thereby optimizing their application and reducing the indiscriminate use of chemicals.94 Moreover, innovative systems like the Pesticide-Fertilizer All-In-One Combination (PFAC) strategy employ deep learning and advanced materials such as hollow mesoporous silica and polydopamine coatings to achieve precision delivery and synergistic effects in pest control and nutrient supply.95 The use of nanocomposites also facilitates the sustained release and targeted delivery of agrochemicals, enhancing plant production and protection while addressing biosafety and environmental concerns.96 Despite these advancements, the field of nano-enabled agriculture is still in its infancy, with ongoing research needed to develop biodegradable, cost-effective, and safe nanomaterials, as well as to conduct systematic studies on nanotoxicity and public awareness.69 The nano-enabled delivery systems hold great promise for creating a more sustainable and efficient agricultural system, but further research and development are essential to fully realize their potential.97

sec.title: Smart Delivery Mechanisms and Release Dynamics
sec.p: Stimuli-responsive nano-delivery systems are innovative approaches in PA, designed to enhance the efficiency and environmental safety of agrichemicals by responding to specific environmental triggers. These systems include pH-responsive, temperature-responsive, moisture-responsive, and enzyme-triggered release mechanisms. pH-responsive systems, such as those utilizing bio-stimulant-based nanocarriers, release their payload in response to the acidic or basic conditions of the target environment, optimizing the delivery of fungicides like tebuconazole and prothioconazole for effective control of Fusarium Head Blight in wheat.98 Temperature-responsive systems, exemplified by poly(N-isopropylacrylamide)-based nanogels, adjust the release rate of pesticides like lambda-cyhalothrin in response to temperature changes, aligning pesticide release with pest population dynamics and improving pest control efficacy while reducing environmental residues.99 Moisture-responsive systems, although not explicitly detailed in the provided contexts, generally rely on the presence of water to trigger the release of active ingredients, ensuring that agrichemicals are only released when conditions are conducive to plant uptake. Enzyme-triggered systems leverage the presence of specific enzymes secreted by pests or pathogens to degrade the carrier material and release the active ingredient, providing targeted action against pests and pathogens while minimizing non-target effects.100 These systems are often constructed using biopolymer-based core-shell nanostructures, which can be tailored for multi-stimuli responsiveness, enhancing the precision of agrichemical delivery and improving plant health metrics such as photosynthesis efficacy and nutrient uptake.101 The integration of these stimuli-responsive mechanisms into nano-delivery systems represents a promising development in sustainable agriculture, offering a means to reduce the indiscriminate use of pesticides and fertilizers, thereby mitigating their environmental and health impacts.65,94 As research progresses, the development of hybrid and multi-stimuli-responsive formulations continues to hold promise for further enhancing the stability, bioavailability, and targeted delivery of agrichemicals, paving the way for more efficient and eco-friendly agricultural practices.102

sec.title: Sustainability and Efficiency of Nano-Delivery Systems
sec.p: Nano-enabled delivery systems have significantly contributed to reducing agrochemical overuse, minimizing environmental losses, improving resource-use efficiency, and supporting sustainable farming practices. These systems, which include nano-fertilizers, nano-pesticides, and nano-herbicides, offer enhanced efficiency and targeted delivery of agrochemicals, thereby reducing the required dosages and minimizing environmental contamination.72,103 For example, nano-fertilizers provide controlled and sustained nutrient release, which reduces leaching and pollution, while enhancing nutrient uptake and plant health.49,72 Similarly, nano-pesticides and herbicides enable precise application, reducing waste and contamination, and improving crop protection.104,105 The use of nano-biosensors further supports sustainable agriculture by enabling real-time monitoring of plant health and environmental conditions, thus optimizing resource usage and enhancing precision farming practices.106,107 Additionally, Si NPs have been shown to improve plant resilience against abiotic stresses such as drought and salinity, further supporting sustainable crop production.49 The integration of nanotechnology into agriculture not only enhances the efficiency of agrochemical use but also aligns with global sustainability goals by reducing the ecological footprint of farming practices.104,108 Despite these advancements, challenges remain, including the need for further research on the long-term environmental impacts and the development of biodegradable and cost-effective nanomaterials.69,109 Overall, nano-enabled delivery systems represent a promising avenue for achieving sustainable agriculture by enhancing productivity while minimizing environmental impacts.

The sustainability benefits of nano-enabled delivery systems also depend on the formulation and conditions of application. Controlled release may reduce input losses and improve delivery efficiency, but this does not necessarily mean that the complete delivery system has a lower environmental burden. Carrier materials, synthesis requirements, formulation stability, degradation products, and end-of-life (EoL) behaviour may introduce additional impacts that are not always considered in short-term agronomic studies. Moreover, the limited commercial application of many nano-enabled systems indicates that laboratory demonstrations of improved delivery efficiency have not yet consistently translated into field-scale benefits. Figure 4 illustrates the mechanisms through which nano-enabled delivery systems improve the efficiency, precision, and sustainability of agricultural inputs in plants. The framework begins with green-synthesized NPs that are formulated as nano-fertilizers, nano-pesticides, nano-herbicides, and advanced nanocarriers possessing biocompatible, biodegradable, and low-toxicity characteristics. These delivery systems enhance agricultural performance through controlled release, targeted delivery, and the use of smart nanocarriers capable of protecting active ingredients, increasing loading capacity, and improving solubility and penetration. The illustration further highlights the importance of stimuli-responsive release mechanisms, where environmental and biological triggers such as pH variations, temperature fluctuations, moisture availability, and enzymatic activity regulate the release of encapsulated compounds according to plant and field requirements. Following root or foliar application, NPs undergo uptake, cellular internalization, vascular translocation, and targeted delivery to specific tissues, where active ingredients are released in a controlled manner. These processes improve nutrient availability, agrochemical utilization, plant protection, and resource-use efficiency while minimizing losses associated with conventional agricultural inputs. The resulting outcomes include enhanced crop productivity, improved disease management, reduced agrochemical consumption, lower environmental contamination, and more sustainable crop production systems. The illustration demonstrates how nano-enabled delivery technologies integrate controlled transport, site-specific release, and intelligent carrier design to support PA and environmentally responsible farming practices.

sec.title: Nano-Biosensors for Soil and Crop Monitoring
sec.p: Nano-biosensors have emerged as a promising approach in precision farming systems, offering promising developments in monitoring soil nutrients, crop health, pathogens, environmental conditions, and agricultural stress factors. These sensors leverage nanotechnology to provide highly sensitive, accurate, and real-time data, which is crucial for optimizing agricultural practices and ensuring sustainable farming. For example, nano-sensors can be seamlessly integrated into plant systems to detect stress signals and environmental conditions, thereby enabling early intervention and precise management of crop health.115,116 In soil nutrient monitoring, nano-biosensors facilitate the efficient use of natural resources by providing detailed insights into soil conditions, which helps in optimizing nutrient application and reducing environmental impacts.117,118 Moreover, these sensors are instrumental in detecting pathogens and managing crop diseases, offering a proactive approach to pest and pathogen control, which is essential for maintaining crop productivity and quality.118,119 The integration of nanotechnology with sensor networks also enhances the detection of environmental pollutants and stress factors, contributing to improved plant growth and stress resistance.120,121 Additionally, the development of plant wearables and wireless sensor networks has expanded the capabilities of PA, allowing for continuous monitoring and data-driven decision-making.116 Despite these advancements, challenges such as biosafety, regulatory issues, and scalability remain, necessitating further research and development to fully harness the potential of nano-biosensors in agriculture.103,121 The application of nano-biosensors in precision farming represents a significant step towards achieving sustainable agriculture by enhancing resource-use efficiency, reducing agrochemical inputs, and supporting environmental conservation.114,122

sec.title: Integration with Precision Farming Technologies
sec.p: The integration of green nanoparticle-based sensing systems with IoT technologies, drones, remote sensing platforms, and real-time agricultural monitoring systems represents a promising development in PA, enhancing efficiency and sustainability. IoT technologies, when combined with drones and UAVs, facilitate comprehensive environmental monitoring by collecting vast amounts of data from both above and below ground, which is then transmitted to cloud platforms for analysis and storage, enabling real-time decision-making and predictive analytics for crop management.123,124 Drones equipped with multispectral and hyperspectral sensors provide high-resolution data for crop monitoring, disease detection, and precision spraying, which are crucial for optimizing resource use and improving crop yields.124,125 The integration of IoT with autonomous robotic systems further enhances PA by enabling site-specific observations and real-time data collection, which are essential for tasks such as canopy mapping and soil moisture monitoring.126 These technologies are complemented by AI and big data analytics, which analyze extensive datasets to uncover patterns and trends, providing valuable insights for improving agricultural practices.127 Moreover, the use of IoT-based sensors in greenhouses allows for precise control of environmental conditions, optimizing plant growth and resource use.128 The integration of beneficial microbes with sensor technologies also contributes to sustainable agriculture by enhancing nutrient cycling and reducing reliance on chemical inputs.120 Despite these advancements, challenges such as sensor calibration, power demands, and regulatory issues for drone operations remain, necessitating ongoing research and collaboration to fully realize the potential of these integrated systems in transforming agriculture.125,126 The synergy between green nanoparticle-based sensing systems and these advanced technologies offers a pathway to more resilient and efficient agricultural systems, addressing global challenges such as climate change and food security.125,129

sec.title: AI-Assisted Smart Farming Systems
sec.p: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) play a pivotal role in optimizing nano-enabled precision farming systems by enhancing predictive analytics, smart irrigation, nutrient management, and automated decision-making. The integration of AI with nanotechnology in PA allows for real-time responses to changes in crop growth, optimizing nutrient uptake and delivery while considering long-term impacts on soil microbial communities.1 Machine learning algorithms, such as deep learning models, are instrumental in processing complex datasets to deliver actionable insights for precision decision-making, including yield prediction, nutrient management, and irrigation optimization.130 These technologies facilitate precise water and fertilizer applications, improving resource use efficiency and minimizing environmental impacts through advanced irrigation methods and predictive modelling.131 The use of IoT-based automated solutions, combined with ML, enhances real-time irrigation management, optimizing water use and maximizing crop yields.132 Moreover, ML-based systems are crucial for developing decision support tools in nutrient management, improving yields while reducing expenses and environmental impact.133 The application of ML in irrigation decision-making has evolved to include crop water need predictions, enhancing accuracy and water conservation compared to traditional methods.134 Additionally, big data and AI technologies are driving a paradigm shift in smart farming, with intelligent decision-making models supporting precise regulation of water, fertilizer, and pest management.135 The convergence of these technologies in PA not only boosts productivity but also addresses global food security challenges by ensuring sustainable and efficient farming practices.136 The strategic integration of AI and ML in precision farming systems represents a promising development in agricultural practices, offering substantial benefits for sustainable agriculture and global food security.

Figure 5 illustrates the integration of nano-biosensors, Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, remote sensing platforms, AI, and machine learning within a unified precision farming framework for real-time agricultural monitoring and decision-making. The system begins with a nano-biosensor network that continuously monitors soil nutrients, crop health, pathogen presence, environmental conditions, and abiotic stress indicators, providing high-resolution field data. These data streams are complemented by IoT sensor networks, UAVs, remote sensing technologies, and plant wearable sensors, which collectively enable large-scale surveillance, early stress detection, disease diagnosis, and continuous crop monitoring. The information generated from these platforms is transmitted to cloud-based infrastructures where data are integrated, stored, processed, and synchronized for large-scale agricultural analytics. AI and machine learning algorithms subsequently transform these datasets into actionable insights through predictive analytics, yield forecasting, nutrient management optimization, irrigation scheduling, anomaly detection, and automated decision support. The resulting intelligence supports precision nutrient management, smart irrigation, targeted pest and disease control, and site-specific crop management practices tailored to field variability and crop requirements. These integrated technologies enhance resource-use efficiency, reduce agrochemical and water inputs, improve crop productivity, support climate-resilient farming, and minimize environmental impacts. The framework demonstrates how nano-enabled sensing technologies combined with digital agriculture tools create a data-driven precision farming ecosystem that supports sustainable agricultural production, real-time management, and informed decision-making across the entire crop production cycle.

sec.title: Uptake and Translocation Pathways
sec.p: The uptake, transport, translocation, and accumulation pathways of green NPs in plants involve complex interactions across root, foliar, and vascular systems. Root uptake is a primary pathway where NPs are absorbed through root hairs and transported via the xylem to aboveground tissues. Studies have shown that NPs such as nano-biochar and polystyrene nanoplastics are readily absorbed by plant roots and translocated to shoots and leaves, with significant accumulation in root cortical and vascular tissues.139,140 The efficiency of this process can vary significantly among plant species, influenced by anatomical and physiological traits.140 Foliar uptake occurs primarily through stomatal and cuticular routes, where NPs penetrate the leaf surface and are transported via apoplastic and symplastic pathways.141,142 The translocation of foliar-applied NPs is facilitated by the phloem, enabling bidirectional movement to roots and other plant parts, although the extent of this movement can be limited by factors such as nanoparticle size, surface charge, and plant species.143,144 Vascular transport involves the movement of NPs through the xylem and phloem, with studies on CeO2 NPs in cucumber plants demonstrating their distribution and transformation within plant tissues.145 The transport and accumulation of NPs are further influenced by environmental conditions and the physical-chemical properties of the NPs, such as size, zeta potential, and affinity to organic phases.141,146 These pathways highlight the potential for NPs to enhance nutrient delivery and crop protection, but also raise concerns about their entry into the food chain and associated health risks, necessitating further research into their long-term implications and safe application in agriculture.139,147

sec.title: Physiological and Biochemical Responses
sec.p: The exposure of plants to green NPs elicits a range of physiological, biochemical, and metabolic responses that significantly impact photosynthesis, enzymatic activity, nutrient assimilation, and stress responses. Green NPs, such as Fe3O4, TiO2, and AgNPs, have been shown to enhance photosynthetic efficiency by increasing chlorophyll content and improving the photosynthetic apparatus, which is crucial for carbon assimilation and overall plant growth.148–150 For example, Fe3O4 NPs have been reported to increase sugar content and photosynthesis in Dendrobium huoshanense, while TiO2 NPs enhance photosynthesis efficiency in Pisum sativum by improving CO2 assimilation and gas exchange parameters.149,150 These NPs also influence enzymatic activities, particularly those involved in antioxidant defense mechanisms. The application of NPs can boost the activities of antioxidant enzymes such as catalase (CAT), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and peroxidase (POD), thereby enhancing the plant’s ability to mitigate oxidative stress induced by environmental factors.73,151 This is particularly evident under drought conditions, where NPs have been shown to reduce oxidative stress markers like malondialdehyde (MDA) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2).151 Moreover, green NPs can alter nutrient assimilation by affecting the uptake and accumulation of essential elements such as Fe, Mn, Co, and Zn, which are vital for various metabolic processes.149,150 However, the impact of NPs is dose-dependent, as excessive concentrations can lead to phytotoxicity, disrupting photosynthesis and increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, as observed with copper oxide NPs in lettuce.152 Despite these challenges, the strategic use of NPs, particularly at optimal concentrations, can enhance plant resilience to stress by modulating stress-responsive pathways and improving overall plant health and productivity.153,154 Thus, while green NPs offer promising benefits for plant growth and stress tolerance, careful consideration of their concentration and type is essential to maximize their positive effects while minimizing potential adverse impacts.

sec.title: Interaction with Soil Microbiome and Rhizosphere
sec.p: Green NPs (NPs) have a multifaceted impact on soil microorganisms, rhizosphere interactions, microbial diversity, and soil ecological balance within sustainable agricultural systems. The effects of NPs on soil microorganisms are highly variable, depending on factors such as NP type, concentration, and soil properties. For example, metal and metal oxide NPs, like Ag and ZnO, can have both stimulatory and inhibitory effects on soil microbiota, with toxicity often increasing at higher concentrations.155–157 These NPs can disrupt key microbial processes such as mineralization and nitrogen fixation, which are crucial for plant growth and soil health.156 However, at lower concentrations, ZnO NPs have been shown to enhance plant growth and microbial activity, indicating a potential for beneficial applications in agriculture.156 The interactions between NPs and soil microorganisms also extend to the rhizosphere, where they can alter microbial community structures and functions. For example, TiO2 NPs have been observed to shift the wheat rhizobiome towards chemoheterotrophy, promoting beneficial plant-associated bacteria.158 Moreover, plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) can facilitate the green synthesis of NPs, which can be used for soil remediation and nutrient delivery, thus supporting sustainable agriculture.159 Despite these potential benefits, the introduction of NPs into soil ecosystems poses risks to microbial diversity and ecological balance. Meta-analyses have shown that NPs can significantly reduce microbial diversity, biomass, and activity, with metal NPs having more pronounced negative effects than carbon-based NPs.155,160 These adverse effects underscore the need for careful assessment and management of NP applications in agriculture to avoid disrupting soil ecological balance.160 Moreover, the integration of nanotechnology with biological processes, such as rhizoremediation, offers promising strategies for enhancing soil health and mitigating pollution, although the ecological risks associated with NP use must be addressed.161,162 While green NPs hold potential for advancing sustainable agricultural practices, their application requires a nuanced understanding of their interactions with soil microorganisms and ecosystems to ensure environmental safety and efficacy.163

Taken together, these findings indicate that the biological effects of NPs cannot be interpreted solely in terms of whether a material is classified as green or non-green. The same nanoparticle may produce beneficial responses at one concentration or under one set of environmental conditions and adverse responses at another. Particle characteristics, exposure conditions, plant species, soil properties, and microbial communities therefore need to be considered when interpreting reported agricultural outcomes. This variability is an important reason why results from individual laboratory studies should not be generalized directly to field-scale agricultural systems. Figure 6 illustrates the pathways through which green NPs enter, move within, and interact with plants, ultimately influencing crop performance and agricultural productivity. The framework highlights two principal routes of nanoparticle entry: root uptake from the rhizosphere and foliar uptake through leaf surfaces. Following absorption, NPs are transported through apoplastic and symplastic pathways, enabling cell-to-cell movement and internal distribution within plant tissues. Long-distance translocation occurs through the vascular system, where xylem transport facilitates upward movement from roots to aerial organs, while phloem transport enables redistribution to metabolically active sink tissues. As NPs accumulate in roots, stems, leaves, reproductive organs, and cellular compartments, they interact with physiological and biochemical processes that regulate nutrient assimilation, photosynthetic activity, water-use efficiency, and stress tolerance. These interactions can stimulate antioxidant defense systems, modulate reactive oxygen species homeostasis, activate stress-responsive pathways, and influence metabolic and hormonal regulation. The illustration also emphasizes the importance of rhizosphere interactions, where NPs affect soil microorganisms, plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria, microbial diversity, and nutrient cycling processes that contribute to soil ecological balance. Collectively, these uptake, transport, accumulation, and interaction mechanisms influence nutrient-use efficiency, crop growth, stress resilience, productivity, and overall agricultural performance. The framework therefore demonstrates how plant-nanoparticle interactions serve as a critical link between nanoparticle application and the agronomic benefits achieved in PA systems.

sec.title: Soil and Water Environmental Impacts
sec.p: The environmental fate, mobility, persistence, and accumulation of green NPs in soil and water systems, particularly in agricultural applications, are complex and multifaceted issues. Green NPs, such as cerium dioxide (CeO2-NPs), copper-based nanomaterials (Cu-based NMs), and magnetic iron-based nanoparticles (MINPs), are increasingly utilized in agriculture due to their potential to enhance crop productivity and resilience against stressors like drought and heavy metal contamination.169,170 However, their release into the environment raises concerns about their long-term ecological impacts. In soil systems, NPs can undergo various transformation processes, including agglomeration, dissolution, and redox reactions, which influence their mobility and bioavailability.171 These transformations can affect the soil’s physico-chemical properties and microbial communities, potentially disrupting plant-microbe interactions essential for plant nutrition and soil health.170,172 NPs can also act as carriers for other pollutants, facilitating the spread of contaminants to adjacent water bodies or groundwater.171 The persistence of NPs in the environment is influenced by their nanoscale size, which complicates their detection and risk assessment.173,174 Studies using models like nanoFate have shown that even soluble metal oxide NPs can accumulate in the environment at concentrations that may exceed toxic thresholds, particularly in high-production scenarios.175 The uptake and translocation of NPs in plants occur through various pathways, including root and foliar adsorption, and are influenced by factors such as soil characteristics and the presence of other ions.176 Despite their potential benefits, the accumulation of NPs in soil and plant systems poses risks to crop production and food security, necessitating further research to understand their environmental behavior and develop guidelines for their safe use in agriculture.172,177 While green NPs offer promising applications in agriculture, their environmental fate and impacts require careful consideration to ensure sustainable agricultural practices.177,178

sec.title: Ecotoxicological Risks and Bioaccumulation
sec.p: The ecotoxicological impacts of green NPs on non-target organisms, aquatic systems, beneficial soil biota, and food-chain bioaccumulation are multifaceted and complex. Zinc oxide NPs have been shown to affect various aquatic organisms, with freshwater invertebrates being particularly sensitive, followed by bacteria, algae, and vertebrates. The primary mechanisms of toxicity include the release of Zn2+ ions and the generation of ROS.179 Similarly, Ag NPs exhibit toxicity in aquatic environments, with bioaccumulation and transformation processes affecting aquatic flora and fauna. The toxicity of biologically synthesized AgNPs is comparable to chemically synthesized ones, impacting aquatic microcosms through various exposure routes.180 The fate of NPs in aquatic and terrestrial environments is influenced by their direct and indirect introduction through industrial discharges and runoff, affecting both water and soil ecosystems.178 The ecotoxicological effects of nanomaterials (NMs) are significant across different environments, with a need for further research to address knowledge gaps and achieve sustainable development goals.181 Studies have shown that crustaceans, algae, and fish are particularly sensitive to Ag, CuO, and ZnO NPs, with potential threats to non-target organisms due to their release from consumer products.182 Metallic nanomaterials (MNMs) can accumulate and transform within aquatic food webs, posing risks of bioaccumulation and biomagnification, although current studies often show biomagnification factors (BMF) of less than 1, indicating limited biomagnification.183 Graphene oxide contamination in aquatic food webs can disrupt digestion and physiological processes, leading to bioaccumulation and potential biomagnification, particularly affecting top-level consumers and human populations reliant on seafood.184 The unique properties of manufactured NPs complicate risk assessments, as their bioavailability and toxicity can be influenced by environmental factors such as water chemistry.185 Engineered NPs like AgNPs and AuNPs induce oxidative stress in aquatic organisms, with environmental factors affecting their aggregation and toxicity.186 Lastly, titanium dioxide (TiO2) NPs have been shown to reduce microbial abundance and plant growth in terrestrial ecosystems, with potential genotoxic effects on aquatic organisms, highlighting the risks of trophic transfer and toxicity in both terrestrial and aquatic environments.187 The ecotoxicological impacts of green NPs are significant, necessitating careful consideration of their environmental release and interactions to mitigate adverse effects on ecosystems and human health.

An important contradiction in the literature is that biological synthesis does not necessarily eliminate the environmental hazards associated with nanoparticle composition. For example, biologically synthesized AgNPs have been reported to show toxicity comparable to chemically synthesized AgNPs under aquatic exposure conditions. This suggests that the environmental behaviour of a nanoparticle is governed not only by the synthesis route but also by its composition, particle characteristics, dose, transformation, and exposure environment. Therefore, claims of improved environmental safety should be supported by nanoparticle-specific ecotoxicological evidence rather than inferred from the use of a green synthesis method alone.

sec.title: Long-Term Sustainability Concerns
sec.p: Long-term sustainability concerns associated with continuous nanoparticle exposure, ecosystem imbalance, environmental persistence, and unintended ecological consequences are multifaceted and complex. Nanoparticles (NPs), due to their unique properties and widespread use, persist in various environmental matrices, leading to bioaccumulation and potential ecological disruptions. For example, Au NPs have been shown to persist in terrestrial environments, affecting soil organisms like Enchytraeus crypticus by reducing reproduction rates over extended exposure periods, highlighting the increased hazards of low concentrations over time.188 Similarly, Ag NPs have been observed to alter community structures in aquatic ecosystems, reducing zooplankton density and increasing phytoplankton biomass, which in turn affects ecosystem respiration and function.189 The persistence and bioaccumulation of NPs in ecosystems pose significant challenges, as their nanoscale size complicates understanding their environmental behavior and toxicity, necessitating comprehensive risk management strategies.174 Moreover, the interaction of NPs with photosynthetic organisms, such as plants and algae, can disrupt growth and health, impacting ecosystem stability and function.190 The chronic exposure to NPs, such as CuO NPs, can lead to population collapse in pest species due to oxidative stress and impaired reproduction, underscoring the need for multigenerational toxicity assessments.191 Additionally, the effects of boron and vanadium NPs on soil organisms reveal varying toxicological impacts depending on exposure duration and concentration, emphasizing the importance of long-term studies for accurate risk assessment.192 The ecological implications of NPs are further complicated by their potential to alter microbial community structures and functions, as seen with AgNPs affecting microbial decomposer communities in streams, which are crucial for nutrient cycling and ecosystem health.193 The unintended ecological consequences of NPs necessitate a holistic understanding of their environmental impacts, advocating for a safer-by-design approach and the integration of long-term and multigenerational studies into risk assessment frameworks to ensure sustainable NP use.194,195

Figure 7 illustrates the environmental pathways, transformation processes, ecological interactions, and potential ecotoxicological consequences associated with the agricultural application of green NPs. Following their use as nano-fertilizers, nano-pesticides, nano-herbicides, and nano-delivery systems, NPs can enter environmental compartments through soil deposition, foliar deposition, irrigation inputs, agricultural runoff, and residual release. Once released, their environmental fate is governed by processes such as transport, persistence, accumulation, dissolution, aggregation, redox transformations, and surface modifications, which collectively influence nanoparticle bioavailability and mobility within soil and water systems. The illustration highlights that these transformed NPs interact with a wide range of ecological receptors, including crop plants, soil microorganisms, plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria, earthworms, beneficial soil biota, aquatic organisms, beneficial insects, and other non-target species. Such interactions may alter microbial diversity, nutrient cycling, enzymatic activities, soil ecological balance, and aquatic ecosystem functions. The framework further emphasizes the potential for nanoparticle accumulation within plants and subsequent trophic transfer through food chains, raising concerns regarding bioaccumulation and biomagnification across higher trophic levels. Long-term sustainability considerations include environmental persistence, ecosystem imbalance, chronic ecological exposure, soil health alterations, and uncertainties regarding cumulative environmental impacts. Consequently, the illustration underscores the importance of comprehensive environmental risk assessment, ecotoxicological evaluation, environmental monitoring, safe-by-design nanoparticle development, regulatory oversight, and responsible agricultural deployment to ensure that the benefits of green nanotechnology are achieved without compromising environmental integrity and ecosystem health.

The table demonstrates that although green NPs are generally considered more environmentally compatible than conventionally synthesized nanomaterials, their behavior after environmental release is influenced by factors such as particle composition, size, surface properties, concentration, and environmental conditions. Following application, NPs may undergo transport, accumulation, dissolution, aggregation, and transformation processes within soil and water environments, affecting their mobility, persistence, bioavailability, and ecological interactions. The data reported highlights that NPs can influence soil microbial communities, nutrient cycling processes, enzymatic activities, rhizosphere functions, and overall soil ecological balance, with effects varying according to nanoparticle type and exposure levels. The potential for plant uptake, trophic transfer, bioaccumulation, and movement through food chains is also emphasized as an important consideration for long-term environmental safety. Despite these concerns, the data indicates that appropriately designed green NPs can reduce agrochemical losses, improve input-use efficiency, minimize pesticide and fertilizer runoff, and lower the environmental footprint of agricultural production when applied responsibly. The findings further underscore the importance of ecotoxicological evaluation, environmental monitoring, safe-by-design nanoparticle development, lifecycle assessment, and regulatory oversight to ensure sustainable deployment. The data reported highlights the need to balance the agronomic benefits of green NPs with careful environmental risk management, supporting the development of PA systems that are both productive and environmentally sustainable.
