sec.title: Circular Agriculture and Waste-Derived Green Nanoparticles
Agro-Waste and Biomass-Derived Nanoparticles
sec.p: The utilization of agricultural residues, food waste, and biomass resources for green nanoparticle synthesis represents a promising development in waste valorization and sustainable resource utilization. Green synthesis methods leverage natural reagents such as plant extracts, microorganisms, and agricultural waste, offering an reduced chemical use alternative to conventional chemical and physical nanoparticle synthesis methods, which are often energy-intensive and environmentally harmful.35,201 Agricultural residues, such as lignocellulosic biomass, are particularly promising due to their abundance and potential to be converted into high-value nanomaterials like nanocellulose and nanolignin, which have applications in packaging, medicine, and energy.202 For example, lignin NPs derived from agricultural residues can be transformed into multifunctional catalytic systems, such as lignin-based magnetic nanocomposites, which are effective in dye removal from wastewater.203 Similarly, fruit and vegetable wastes, such as Citrus limetta peels and potato peels, have been used to synthesize iron oxide and silver NPs, respectively, demonstrating excellent catalytic and antimicrobial properties.204,205 These NPs not only offer potential applications in environmental remediation and medicine but also contribute to sustainable waste management by converting waste into valuable products.205 Moreover, the synthesis of silica NPs from agricultural waste, particularly from silica-rich residues like cereal crops, highlights the potential for agro-waste management and valorization, with applications in biomedicine and environmental remediation.206,207 The green synthesis of NPs from biomass not only reduces the carbon footprint and energy consumption but also enhances the economic viability of nanoparticle production by utilizing low-cost, renewable resources.30,45 The integration of green synthesis methods in nanoparticle production underscores the importance of sustainable practices in advancing nanotechnology and addressing global environmental challenges.30,35

sec.title: Resource Recovery and Circular Farming Systems
sec.p: Green NPs play a pivotal role in supporting circular agriculture by enhancing nutrient recycling, resource recovery, waste minimization, and closed-loop farming systems. These NPs, synthesized through eco-friendly methods, offer a sustainable alternative to traditional agricultural inputs like fertilizers and pesticides, thereby reducing environmental impact and promoting resource efficiency.48,208 Green nanomaterials, such as nanofertilizers and nanopesticides, are designed to improve soil health and plant productivity by enhancing nutrient uptake and stress resistance, which are crucial for nutrient cycling and soil microbial diversity.209,210 The use of biological resources in the synthesis of these NPs minimizes the production of hazardous substances and energy input, aligning with the principles of circular agriculture.45 Moreover, nanotechnology facilitates the valorization of agricultural waste into high-value products, such as biofuels and bio-based compounds, thus supporting resource recovery and waste minimization.211 The integration of nanotechnology in precision farming allows for targeted delivery of nutrients and pesticides, optimizing their use and reducing environmental pollution.103,163 Additionally, the development of graphene from agricultural waste exemplifies how nanotechnology can transform waste into valuable materials, further closing the loop in agricultural systems.212 Despite these advancements, there are concerns regarding the potential toxicity and environmental impact of NPs, necessitating robust risk assessment and management strategies to ensure their safe and effective use in agriculture.208,213 The green NPs offer promising solutions for advancing circular agriculture by enhancing sustainability and efficiency across various agricultural processes.

Waste-derived nanoparticle production also involves important trade-offs. Although the use of agricultural residues can reduce waste disposal and provide low-cost feedstocks, the overall sustainability of the process depends on feedstock collection, transportation, pre-treatment, extraction efficiency, synthesis yield, energy requirements, and the management of residual materials. Variability in waste composition may also affect nanoparticle properties and reproducibility. Therefore, waste valorization should not automatically be equated with circularity; its environmental and economic benefits need to be demonstrated across the complete production chain.

sec.title: Sustainable Nanomanufacturing for Agriculture
sec.p: Sustainable and scalable nanomanufacturing approaches in agriculture emphasize eco-friendly production, circular resource utilization, and environmentally responsible practices. Nanotechnology offers transformative solutions for sustainable agriculture by enhancing crop productivity, improving soil health, and ensuring efficient resource utilization. For example, nanoscale delivery systems, such as polymer-based NPs and metal oxide particles, enable precise application of fertilizers and pesticides, reducing environmental impact and optimizing nutrient use.43,103 The integration of nanotechnology with digital agriculture platforms facilitates real-time monitoring and adaptive management, further supporting sustainable practices.103 Biogenic synthesis of NPs, using plant extracts and microorganisms, presents an potentially lower-impact alternative to conventional methods, offering benefits such as cost-effectiveness, scalability, and biocompatibility.214 This green synthesis aligns with the principles of the circular economy by promoting waste valorization and resource efficiency, as seen in the conversion of organic waste into biofuels using nanocatalysts.211 Additionally, nanotechnology aids in pollution detection and stress resistance, enhancing plant growth and resilience while minimizing agrochemical use.121 However, challenges such as nanopollution, nanotoxicity, and regulatory issues must be addressed to ensure responsible deployment.215,216 The development of biodegradable nanomaterials and standardized guidelines for evaluating nanomaterial toxicity are crucial for mitigating potential risks.103,208 Collaborative efforts among researchers, policymakers, and stakeholders are essential to harness the full potential of nanotechnology for sustainable agricultural growth, ensuring food security and environmental stewardship for future generations.119,211

Figure 8 presents a circular agriculture framework that integrates agricultural waste valorization, green nanoparticle synthesis, precision farming applications, and sustainable resource management within a closed-loop agricultural system. The framework begins with diverse agricultural and biomass waste streams, including crop residues, fruit and vegetable wastes, agro-processing residues, food wastes, lignocellulosic biomass, and agricultural by-products, which are transformed from disposal burdens into valuable feedstocks through resource recovery and waste-to-resource conversion processes. These recovered materials serve as renewable substrates for the green synthesis of NPs through plant-mediated, microbial, and biomolecule-assisted pathways, leading to the production of value-added nanomaterials such as silver, iron oxide, silica, zinc oxide, carbon-based, and lignin-derived NPs. The resulting waste-derived NPs support multiple PA applications, including nano-fertilizers, nano-pesticides, nano-enabled nutrient delivery systems, crop protection technologies, stress management strategies, and resource-efficient farming practices. The framework further demonstrates that these applications contribute to enhanced nutrient recycling, reduced input losses, improved resource utilization, reduced agrochemical dependence, lower environmental pollution, decreased waste disposal requirements, and reduced carbon emissions. These benefits collectively support sustainable nanomanufacturing through eco-friendly production processes, scalable manufacturing systems, circular resource utilization, and reduced energy demand. Ultimately, the integration of waste valorization, green nanotechnology, and PA creates a circular agricultural ecosystem characterized by closed-loop resource flows, agricultural waste minimization, sustainable food production, circular bioeconomy development, and improved long-term agricultural sustainability. The return of biomass residues back into the agricultural production cycle reinforces the circularity of the system, demonstrating how waste-derived green NPs can simultaneously support productivity, environmental protection, and resource conservation objectives in sustainable farming systems.

The table demonstrates that a wide range of agricultural wastes, including crop residues, fruit and vegetable wastes, agro-industrial by-products, food-processing residues, lignocellulosic biomass, and algal biomass, can serve as renewable feedstocks for the green synthesis of NPs. Through plant-mediated, microbial, and biomolecule-assisted synthesis pathways, these waste resources are converted into functional nanomaterials such as silver, zinc oxide, iron oxide, silica, carbon-based, and lignin-derived NPs with applications in PA. The synthesized NPs contribute to nano-fertilization, nano-pesticide formulations, controlled nutrient delivery, crop protection, stress management, and enhanced resource-use efficiency, thereby improving agricultural productivity while reducing dependence on conventional agrochemical inputs. The data reported further emphasizes the circular economy benefits associated with waste valorization, including nutrient recovery, resource recycling, waste minimization, reduced environmental pollution, and lower carbon footprints. By converting agricultural waste streams into high-value agricultural inputs, these approaches create closed-loop production systems that enhance sustainability across the agricultural value chain. In addition, the integration of waste-derived NPs with sustainable nanomanufacturing practices promotes eco-friendly production, scalable resource utilization, and reduced energy and material consumption. The data reported demonstrates that waste-derived green NPs represent an important link between circular bioeconomy principles and PA, enabling the simultaneous achievement of waste management, resource recovery, environmental protection, and sustainable food production objectives.

sec.title: Technical and Field-Level Challenges
sec.p: The practical implementation of green NPs in PA faces several technical and field-level challenges, as highlighted across the provided papers. One significant challenge is the reproducibility of green synthesis methods, which, although eco-friendly and cost-effective, often suffer from variability in nanoparticle size and properties due to the inherent complexity of biological systems used in synthesis.214 Scalability of nanoparticle production is another hurdle, as many green synthesis methods are not yet optimized for large-scale production, limiting their practical application in agriculture.251 Field conditions introduce variability that affects the consistency of nanoparticle performance; factors such as soil type, climate, and crop species can influence the efficacy of NPs, complicating the development of standardized application protocols.22 Nanoparticle stability and shelf life are also critical concerns, as many green NPs may degrade or lose functionality over time, impacting their effectiveness in field applications.109 Delivery efficiency is another challenge, with the need for advanced delivery systems that ensure targeted and controlled release of NPs to maximize their benefits while minimizing environmental impact.103 Plant-nanoparticle interactions are complex and not fully understood, with potential risks of toxicity and unintended effects on plant physiology and soil microbiota.70 Finally, achieving consistent agronomic performance under diverse environmental and cropping systems remains elusive, as NPs may perform well under controlled conditions but fail to deliver the same results in variable field environments.72 Addressing these challenges requires interdisciplinary research, improved synthesis techniques, and robust regulatory frameworks to ensure the safe and effective use of green NPs in agriculture.32,33

sec.title: Economic Feasibility and Commercialization
sec.p: The economic feasibility and commercialization potential of green nanoparticle-based agricultural technologies are influenced by several factors, including production costs, availability of biomass-derived feedstocks, and scalability of green synthesis processes. The use of lignocellulosic biomass for nanoparticle production is promising due to its biodegradability and broad applicability, but challenges such as high energy requirements and low product stability persist, impacting economic viability.202,252 The availability of biomass-derived feedstocks is abundant, with agro-industrial waste offering a sustainable source for cellulose and lignin extraction, although the efficiency of these processes is contingent on the feedstock composition and pre-treatment strategies.253 Green synthesis methods, such as those using plant extracts and microbes, offer reduced chemical use alternatives to conventional nanoparticle production, but scalability remains a challenge due to variability in raw materials and process reproducibility.254 In terms of cost-benefit considerations for precision farming applications, NPs like Ag/AgCl derived from ginger straw waste have shown effective antimicrobial properties against soil-borne pathogens, suggesting potential for reducing agrochemical use and enhancing crop protection.255 However, farmer adoption barriers include the high initial costs and the need for technical knowledge to integrate these technologies into existing farming practices.256 Market readiness is advancing, with bio-based fertilizers and other green technologies projected to grow significantly, driven by regulatory support and circular economy policies.257 Moreover, challenges such as biosafety concerns, regulatory gaps, and the need for standardized testing protocols hinder large-scale industrial deployment.256,258 While green nanoparticle-based agricultural technologies hold significant promise for sustainable agriculture, their commercialization will require overcoming technical, economic, and regulatory hurdles through integrated approaches and industry-academia partnerships.256,259

sec.title: Regulatory and Safety Considerations
sec.p: The agricultural use of green NPs presents several regulatory and safety challenges that necessitate comprehensive frameworks for risk assessment and management. Although international guidance and testing approaches for nanomaterial characterization, environmental fate and risk assessment are available, important gaps remain in their harmonized application to agricultural nanomaterials, particularly under realistic field conditions.249,260 The complexity of nanoparticle interactions in agricultural settings, such as their mobility, transformation, and interaction with soil components, further complicates the assessment of their ecological risks.260 Toxicity testing protocols must be refined to account for the unique properties of NPs, including their size, surface chemistry, and potential for bioaccumulation, which can influence their toxicity and environmental persistence.261,262 Additionally, the integration of NPs into PA raises food safety concerns, as their transfer from soils to edible plant tissues could pose risks to human health.263 Public acceptance of nano-enabled technologies is another critical factor, as societal concerns about the safety and ethical implications of nanotechnology can influence regulatory decisions and market adoption.264 To address these challenges, there is a pressing need for regulatory harmonization and the development of internationally recognized safety standards that support innovation while ensuring environmental and human health.265 Policy measures should focus on fostering collaboration between researchers, industry stakeholders, and regulatory bodies to align scientific advancements with regulatory frameworks.266 This includes the establishment of platforms like MIND, which aim to integrate fragmented initiatives and promote knowledge sharing across disciplines.266 Ultimately, a balanced approach that considers both the benefits and potential risks of NPs is essential for their safe and sustainable integration into agriculture, ensuring that technological advancements do not compromise ecological integrity or public health.267,268

Current regulatory approaches to agricultural nanotechnology are largely implemented through existing chemical, pesticide, fertiliser, food and environmental legislation rather than through a single regulatory system specifically dedicated to agricultural nanomaterials.269,270 In the European Union, nanomaterials are covered by nano-specific provisions under the REACH framework, while nano-enabled plant protection products are addressed within the existing plant protection product regulatory framework, although important gaps remain in relation to nanoforms.270,271 For nanofertilisers, recent evidence indicates that the European Union still lacks a fully fit-for-purpose regulatory pathway specifically adapted to their development and assessment.272 Food and feed applications involving NPs fall within the scope of EFSA safety assessment, with requirements addressing physicochemical characterisation, dietary exposure and, where relevant, nano-specific hazard assessment.273 At the international level, OECD test approaches and guidance have been developed for nanomaterial characterisation and environmental fate, including dissolution, aggregation and transformation processes.274 However, applying these frameworks to agricultural NPs remains challenging because particle size, surface properties, dissolution, transformation, aggregation and environmental conditions can influence their mobility, bioavailability and toxicity.271,274 Greater harmonisation of testing requirements, environmental monitoring and regulatory criteria is therefore needed to support consistent risk assessment and responsible deployment of nano-enabled agricultural products.270–272

sec.title: Technology Readiness Levels, Commercialization Pathways and Industrial Scale-Up
sec.p: Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs) provide a useful framework for distinguishing laboratory research from technologies that have progressed toward agricultural use. The framework consists of nine levels, with TRL 1–3 covering discovery and proof of concept, TRL 4–6 covering testing, validation and prototype development, TRL 7–8 covering demonstration, and TRL 9 representing commercial deployment.275,276 For green NPs in PA, most of the literature remains at the discovery stage. Plant-mediated ZnO, Ag and TiO2 NPs are being investigated for agricultural applications, but inconsistent control of particle size, shape and product quality remains a major barrier to commercial translation.10,14,277 During development, evidence becomes stronger through controlled and semi-realistic validation. For example, 25 nm ZnO NPs produced 85% higher zinc uptake efficiency in tomato than zinc sulfate, while nano-fertilizer studies reported improvements in crop yield and nutrient-use efficiency.22,241 Nano-biosensors for detecting plant stress, pathogens and pesticide residues are also mainly in development, although field trials, farmer education, portability and cost-effectiveness remain important requirements.18 Field demonstration is less common but increasing. A multi-location nano urea study across 21 locations in India reported grain-yield increases of 7.6–9.1% across four zones, with a potential 25% reduction in nitrogen use and an estimated annual reduction of 5.06 billion kg CO2-equivalent emissions.278 In lowland rice, biogenic urea NPs allowed at least 25% of conventional urea to be substituted without harming soil bacterial and fungal species.279 Crop-protection technologies are also progressing toward field validation. Nanoencapsulated lufenuron achieved more than 76% control in semi-field trials and released the active compound up to eight times more slowly than free lufenuron.280 A protein-gated mesoporous silica-λ-cyhalothrin formulation was scaled up for field efficacy testing, while a unimolecular nanopesticide system of approximately 3 nm demonstrated field-scale efficacy against multiple pests.281,282 Commercial deployment remains narrow and is concentrated mainly in nutrient delivery. Nanofertilizers have already been adopted in India, while nano-nitrogen, nano-zinc and nano-copper are under initial testing.283 However, commercialization is not equivalent to widespread adoption because awareness, health concerns, climatic influences, technological limitations and product-quality issues can affect uptake of nano urea.284 Nano-biosensors and many nano-formulated pesticides remain mainly at laboratory or pilot scale.285 Two commercialization pathways are identified: incumbent-led integration through established fertilizer or agrochemical manufacturers and research-led translation through research institutes, spin-outs and consortia.245,281,283 Industrial scale-up remains difficult because biological feedstocks vary with species, geographical origin, growing conditions, season and extraction method, affecting particle size, morphology and surface charge.277,286,287 Differences in precursor concentration, pH, temperature and reaction time can further alter nanoparticle properties, reducing batch-to-batch reproducibility and manufacturing consistency.5,288 High synthesis and characterization costs, together with raw-material and processing costs, further constrain commercial production.16,289 The evidence indicates a strong discovery and development base, a smaller but growing field-demonstration stage, and a narrow commercial segment. Progress toward the sustainable PA objectives of this review will depend on improved manufacturing consistency, field validation, regulatory alignment, economic feasibility and responsible translation from research to agricultural practice.

sec.title: Future Perspectives
sec.p: The integration of green NPs with AI and other advanced technologies presents significant opportunities for enhancing PA, making it more intelligent, scalable, and sustainable. Green NPs, such as those synthesized using plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR), can be utilized for soil remediation and targeted nutrient delivery, thereby improving soil health and resilience against environmental stressors like drought and salinity.159 When combined with AI, these NPs can enhance decision-making processes in PA by providing real-time data on soil conditions and crop health, which can be further optimized using machine learning algorithms and IoT technologies.290 The use of AI in PA, particularly through agentic AI and federated learning, allows for the integration of distributed sensing devices and intelligent agents, enabling real-time monitoring and decision support at the farm level.291 This integration can be further enhanced by incorporating UAVs and satellite remote sensing, which provide high-resolution data for crop health monitoring and landscape analysis, thereby improving resource use efficiency and reducing environmental impact.130 Additionally, the use of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) in agriculture offers potential for pollutant remediation and controlled agrochemical release, which can be optimized through AI-assisted design and multifunctional integration.258 The development of biosensing technologies for pathogen detection, coupled with AI and IoT, facilitates predictive diagnostics and precision crop management, reducing chemical dependency and enhancing climate resilience.292 Moreover, the adoption of bio-based fertilizers derived from waste streams supports circular agricultural practices by improving soil properties and reducing environmental impacts, which can be integrated with AI-driven optimization for enhanced nutrient recovery and climate-adaptive formulations.257 The convergence of these technologies offers a pathway to sustainable PA, addressing challenges such as climate change, resource scarcity, and food security while promoting a circular economy and resilient farming systems.

Recent advances are extending the role of AI from farm management to the design and application of agricultural nanomaterials. Machine learning, deep learning and reinforcement learning can support the design and optimisation of nanocarriers, nano-fertilisers, nano-pesticides and nano-sensing platforms by linking material properties with biological and delivery performance. At the farm level, the integration of nano-biosensors, IoT networks, UAVs, satellite and other remote-sensing systems can provide continuous information on soil nutrients, moisture, crop health, pathogens and environmental conditions. These data can be processed through AI models and smart decision-support systems to improve irrigation scheduling, nutrient application, disease detection and site-specific crop management. Such integration represents a shift towards a continuous sense-analyse-respond agricultural system, although reliable datasets, sensor performance, system interoperability, model transparency and validation under diverse field conditions remain important challenges.130,293,294

Figure 9 presents a future roadmap for the advancement of sustainable nano-enabled PA by integrating technological innovation, environmental stewardship, circular resource management, and responsible governance. The framework builds upon the current foundation established through green-synthesized NPs, smart crop management strategies, nano-enabled delivery systems, nano-biosensors, environmental sustainability initiatives, and circular agriculture practices. It identifies key challenges that must be addressed for large-scale implementation, including reproducibility and scalability of green synthesis processes, field-level performance variability, nanoparticle stability, economic feasibility, commercialization barriers, regulatory compliance, environmental risk assessment, and public acceptance. To overcome these limitations, the framework highlights the growing role of enabling technologies such as AI, machine learning, Internet of Things platforms, UAV-assisted agriculture, remote sensing systems, and cloud-based data analytics, which collectively support data-driven and automated agricultural management. These technologies facilitate the development of advanced nano-delivery systems, intelligent sensing networks, and AI-assisted decision-support platforms capable of optimizing nutrient management, irrigation scheduling, pest control, and crop productivity. The roadmap further emphasizes the importance of next-generation sustainable nanomaterials, including biodegradable, low-toxicity, multifunctional, waste-derived, and safe-by-design NPs, alongside circular agriculture approaches focused on agro-waste valorization, nutrient recycling, resource recovery, and circular nanomanufacturing. The framework also recognizes that long-term adoption requires standardized characterization protocols, comprehensive nanotoxicity assessments, environmental monitoring, harmonized regulatory frameworks, stakeholder engagement, and supportive policy development. Collectively, these advancements are expected to promote climate-resilient farming, site-specific crop management, improved resource-use efficiency, reduced environmental footprints, enhanced food security, sustainable agricultural productivity, and stronger integration of circular bioeconomy principles. The roadmap therefore illustrates a holistic pathway through which green nanotechnology can evolve from emerging agricultural applications to a mature, sustainable, and widely adopted component of future precision farming systems.

sec.title: Critical Analysis and Discussion
sec.p: The evidence reviewed in this study shows that the performance of green NPs depends on several factors and cannot be explained by the type of nanoparticle alone. Dose, particle size, surface properties, method of application, crop type, soil condition and environmental factors can all affect the final outcome. The same nanoparticle may therefore produce a useful response at one concentration but cause harmful effects at a higher concentration. For this reason, the use of green NPs in agriculture should be based on their intended function and application conditions rather than on the general assumption that they are safe because they are produced by a green method.

Metal NPs, particularly silver and copper NPs, show clear potential for disease and pathogen control. However, their effects can change greatly with dose. For example, silver NPs at 100 ppm produced a stimulatory response, whereas 200 ppm reduced maize growth, chlorophyll content and the uptake of phosphorus, magnesium and potassium. Exposure of soil bacteria to 1–10 mg/kg of silver NPs also reduced bacterial diversity by 15–40% within 30 days. These findings highlight an important trade-off. Strong antimicrobial activity may help control harmful microorganisms, but the same property may also affect beneficial microorganisms that are important for soil health and nutrient cycling. Therefore, the effective dose for crop protection may not always be the safest dose for the wider soil environment. More work is needed to identify concentration ranges that provide the required agricultural benefit while limiting damage to non-target organisms.

Metal oxide NPs show an even wider range of responses. Some can provide nutrients, support plant growth, reduce stress or help immobilize contaminants in soil, while others may negatively affect nutrient cycling or plant nutrient uptake. NiFe2O4 at 50 mg/kg increased 1000-seed weight by 12.3% and total yield by 15.6%, showing that some metal oxide systems can provide measurable agronomic benefits. In contrast, CuO reduced nitrification by 25–50%, while TiO2 reduced nutrient uptake efficiency by 10–30% in reported studies. These differences are important because they show that metal oxide NPs cannot be considered as one uniform group. Their environmental effects are strongly influenced by their composition, size, surface characteristics, concentration and interaction with soil and plants. Future studies should therefore evaluate individual materials rather than making broad conclusions about all metal oxide NPs.

Silica NPs appear particularly useful where controlled delivery is required. Their high surface area and tunable structure allow active ingredients to be carried and released over time. A mesoporous silica-chlorfenapyr formulation, for example, provided sustained release for two weeks and produced 57.2% mortality compared with 42.1% for a commercial suspension. This suggests that nanoscale delivery can improve the efficiency of some agricultural chemicals. However, better delivery does not automatically mean better overall performance. A practical formulation must also remain stable during storage, be suitable for large-scale production, release the active ingredient at the required rate and behave predictably after application to soil or plants. The long-term environmental fate of the carrier should also be considered before large-scale use.

Polymeric and biopolymer NPs show considerable promise because they can be used for controlled delivery and are generally designed to improve the stability and handling of agricultural inputs. Reported results include increases of 40.6% in antioxidant enzyme activity, 77.9% in defense enzyme activity, 103.2% in defense-gene expression, 28.1% in biomass and 15.7% in yield. An alginate/chitosan system also achieved more than 50% encapsulation, while PLA-based systems showed high encapsulation efficiency. These results indicate that polymer-based systems can support both crop protection and stress management. At the same time, much of the available evidence is still based on laboratory or controlled experiments. Performance under open-field conditions may be different because temperature, rainfall, soil properties, microbial activity and other environmental factors can change release behaviour and effectiveness. Production cost, raw material consistency, storage stability and regulatory requirements also need further study.

Selenium NPs have a different role from many of the other systems reviewed. Their main value appears to be related to stress tolerance, plant defense and biofortification. They have been associated with the activation of stress-responsive pathways and improved plant responses under adverse conditions. However, the available evidence does not provide a numerical effect size that can be directly compared with the quantitative results reported for several other nanoparticle systems. This is an important evidence gap. In addition, selenium has a relatively narrow range between an effective concentration and an excessive concentration. Future research should therefore focus on identifying suitable dose ranges for different crops and on determining how repeated applications influence selenium accumulation in soil and edible plant tissues.

Carbon-based nanomaterials also show promising results, but their effects are strongly material- and dose-dependent. At 100 µg/mL, graphene oxide increased crop height by 41%, compared with 33% for CNTs and 40% for functionalized CNTs. Carbon dots at 240 mg/L reduced tobacco gray mould by 44%. These results demonstrate the potential of carbon-based materials for plant growth and disease management. However, the reported values should not be treated as a direct comparison of overall performance because the studies used different materials, crops, concentrations and experimental conditions. The possible persistence of some carbon materials, dose-dependent toxicity, production cost and difficulties in large-scale manufacturing also remain concerns.

A major issue across the literature is the gap between promising experimental results and practical field application. Many studies report positive effects under controlled conditions, but fewer studies examine long-term use across different soils, climates, crops and farming systems. There is also limited information on repeated application, accumulation, movement through soil and water, effects on beneficial microorganisms, transfer through the food chain and impacts on non-target organisms. These issues are particularly important for agricultural use because NPs may remain in the production environment after the initial treatment.

Economic feasibility and technology readiness are factors that should receive greater attention. A nanoparticle may perform well in the laboratory but have limited agricultural value if it is expensive to produce, store, transport or scale. TRL assessment helps distinguish laboratory research from field-validated and commercial technologies. Green synthesis can reduce chemical use and allow waste-derived materials, but this does not automatically make the final product inexpensive. Feedstock availability, process consistency, purification, energy requirements, formulation and quality control influence cost. Commercialization may involve manufacturers or research-led translation through institutes, spin-outs and consortia. Future studies should report production cost and scale-up requirements alongside biological effectiveness.

The literature supports green NPs as promising tools for PA, but the evidence does not support treating them as automatically safe, economical or ready for widespread field use. The key need is to move technologies from discovery and development towards field demonstration and commercial deployment through well-designed trials examining benefits and risks. Researchers should report particle size, surface properties, concentration, formulation and application method and evaluate crop performance together with environmental safety, stability, cost, scalability and manufacturing reproducibility. Regulatory requirements should also be considered. This approach would provide a stronger basis for determining which technologies can progress from laboratory research to agricultural practice and where further evidence remains necessary.

list-item.p: Green synthesis using plants, microorganisms, biomolecules, and agricultural wastes can reduce the use of conventional chemical inputs in nanoparticle production.

Green NPs show potential for nutrient delivery, crop protection, stress management, growth promotion, and targeted agrochemical delivery, but their performance depends on nanoparticle properties, dose, crop, soil, and environmental conditions.
Nano-fertilizers, nano-pesticides, nano-herbicides, and controlled-release nanocarriers can improve nutrient-use efficiency and reduce input losses under suitable application conditions.
Nano-biosensors combined with AI, IoT, UAVs, remote sensing, and machine learning can support real-time crop monitoring and site-specific decision-making.
Plant-nanoparticle interactions influence uptake, translocation, physiological responses, and rhizosphere processes, with both beneficial and adverse effects reported.
Environmental fate, phytotoxicity, effects on beneficial microorganisms, bioaccumulation, persistence, and long-term ecosystem impacts remain important concerns.
Waste-derived NPs and circular nanomanufacturing offer opportunities for agricultural waste valorization, resource recovery, and waste reduction.
Most applications remain at laboratory or development stages, while fewer technologies have reached field demonstration and commercial adoption.
This review integrates green nanoparticle synthesis, precision crop management, nano-enabled delivery systems, nano-biosensors, environmental implications, circular agriculture, and digital farming.
The review critically examines the benefits and limitations of major nanoparticle platforms under different agricultural conditions.
It highlights the importance of nanoparticle size, surface properties, concentration, formulation, application method, crop type, and environmental conditions in determining performance.
The review links green nanotechnology with AI, IoT, UAVs, remote sensing, and circular resource management within PA.
It also addresses technology readiness, commercialization, manufacturing consistency, economic feasibility, environmental safety, and regulatory requirements.
Long-term and multi-location field studies are needed to confirm performance, consistency, environmental safety, and scalability under real farming conditions.
Future research should focus on safe-by-design, biodegradable or environmentally compatible, multifunctional, and well-characterized nanoparticle systems.
Standardized methods for synthesis, characterization, toxicity assessment, environmental monitoring, and performance evaluation are needed to improve reproducibility.
Nano-biosensors should be further integrated with AI, IoT, UAVs, remote sensing, and decision-support systems for real-time and site-specific crop management.
Economic studies should include production cost, scale-up, storage, transport, formulation, and quality-control requirements alongside biological performance.
Regulatory approaches should address environmental fate, toxicity, food safety, product quality, and responsible agricultural use.

Collaboration among researchers, farmers, industry, regulators, and policymakers will be essential to move promising technologies from laboratory research toward safe, practical, and economically feasible agricultural applications.
